sections.normalized_html:

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v)] parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: x^2z-2y+z=6.] What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{r}?]
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v) =\big\langle u, \: v, \: \text{_____} \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v)] parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as
[MATH: x^2z-2y+z=6.]
What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{r}?]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form [MATH: z=f(x,y)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: x^{2}z − 2y + z|= 6; (x^{2} + 1)z|= 6 + 2y; z|= (2(y + 3))/(x^{2} + 1)]

Now, a point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \left\langle x, \: y, \: \dfrac{2(y+3)}{x^2+1} \right\rangle.]

Finally, setting [MATH: x=u] and [MATH: y=v,] we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v) =\left\langle u, \: v, \: {\color{black}\dfrac{2(v+3)}{u^2+1}} \right\rangle]

Therefore, the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{r}] is [MATH: {\color{black}\dfrac{2(v+3)}{u^2+1}}.]

items.title: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined in Cylindrical Polar Coordinates

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) =\big\langle r\cos{\theta}, \: r\sin{\theta}, \: \text{_____} \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta)] parametrizes the surface defined in cylindrical polar coordinates as [MATH: {r^2}-4z^2=0] for [MATH: z \geq 0.] What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) =\big\langle r\cos{\theta}, \: r\sin{\theta}, \: \text{_____} \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta)] parametrizes the surface defined in cylindrical polar coordinates as
[MATH: {r^2}-4z^2=0]
for [MATH: z \geq 0.] What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form [MATH: z=f(r,\theta)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: r^{2} − 4z^{2}|= 0; 4z^{2}|= r^{2}; z^{2}|= (r^{2})/(4); z|= (r)/(2)]

We disregard the negative solution since we are given that [MATH: z\geq 0.]

If [MATH: (r, \theta, z)] are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and [MATH: (x,y,z)] are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

[MATH: x = r\cos\theta, \qquad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad z = z.]

Now, a point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

[MATH: \mathbf{f} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \big\langle r\cos\theta, \: r\sin\theta, \: z \big\rangle.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: z= \dfrac r2,] we obtain

[MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) =\left\langle r\cos{\theta}, \: r\sin{\theta}, \: {\color{black} \dfrac r2} \right\rangle.]

Therefore, the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{black} \dfrac r2}.]

sections.normalized_html:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: \theta \sin\theta \sin^2 \phi, \: \theta \sin\phi \cos\phi \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)] parametrizes the surface defined in spherical polar coordinates as [MATH: \rho=\theta \sin{\phi}.] What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]
sections.readable_text:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi) = \big\langle \text{_____}, \: \theta \sin\theta \sin^2 \phi, \: \theta \sin\phi \cos\phi \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(\theta,\phi)] parametrizes the surface defined in spherical polar coordinates as
[MATH: \rho=\theta \sin{\phi}.]
What is the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

sections.normalized_html:
If [MATH: (\rho, \theta, \phi)] are the spherical coordinates of a point, then its Cartesian coordinates [MATH: (x,y,z)] can be found by using the following formulas: [MATH: x = \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \qquad y = \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \qquad z = \rho\cos\phi]

Now, a point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

[MATH: \mathbf{f} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \big\langle \rho\cos\theta\sin\phi, \: \rho\sin\theta\sin\phi, \: \rho\cos\phi \big\rangle.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: \rho=\theta \sin{\phi},] we obtain

[MATH: f(θ, ϕ)|= ⟨θ\sin ϕ ⋅ \cos θ\sin ϕ, θ\sin ϕ ⋅ \sin θ\sin ϕ, θ\sin ϕ ⋅ \cos ϕ⟩; = ⟨θ\cos θ\sin^{2} ϕ, θ\sin θ\sin^{2} ϕ, θ\sin ϕ\cos ϕ⟩.]

Therefore, the first component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{black}\theta \cos\theta \sin^2 \phi}.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Just as a curve in three-dimensional space can be described using a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf r(t)] of a single parameter [MATH: t,] we can also describe a surface in three-dimensional space using a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v)] of two parameters [MATH: u] and [MATH: v.]

Content:
For example, consider the vector-valued function given by

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v) =\langle \cos u, \: v, \: \sin u + 1 \rangle, \qquad
0\leq u \leq \dfrac{\pi}2, \quad -2\leq v \leq 2.]

Content:
The domain of the parameter space [MATH: D] and surface [MATH: S] described by [MATH: \mathbf r(u,v)] are both shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/c2991f33514c09b97ece2de694199bb4]

Content:
As we vary [MATH: (u, v),] the tip of the vector [MATH: \mathbf r(u,v)] touches different points on the surface [MATH: S.] Each choice of point [MATH: (u,v)] in [MATH: D] gives a unique point on [MATH: S,] and varying [MATH: (u,v)] throughout its entire domain traces out the entire surface [MATH: S.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Explicit Cartesian Equation

Example Prompt:
Find a vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v)] that parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as [MATH: z=y^5-x^2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

[MATH: \mathbf{r} = x \, \mathbf{i} + y \, \mathbf{j} + z \, \mathbf{k} = x \, \mathbf{i} + y \, \mathbf{j} + \big(y^5-x^2\big) \, \mathbf{k}.]

Now, setting [MATH: x=u] and [MATH: y=v,] we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v) = u \, \mathbf{i} + v \, \mathbf{j} + \big(v^5-u^2\big) \, \mathbf{k}]

---

Item 5 — Example: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined by an Implicit Cartesian Equation

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v) =\big\langle u, \: v, \: \text{_____} \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v)] parametrizes the surface defined in Cartesian coordinates as
[MATH: x^2z-2y+z=6.]
What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{r}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form [MATH: z=f(x,y)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: x^{2}z − 2y + z|= 6; (x^{2} + 1)z|= 6 + 2y; z|= (2(y + 3))/(x^{2} + 1)]

Now, a point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

[MATH: \mathbf{r} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \left\langle x, \: y, \: \dfrac{2(y+3)}{x^2+1} \right\rangle.]

Finally, setting [MATH: x=u] and [MATH: y=v,] we obtain the vector function that parametrizes the surface:

[MATH: \mathbf{r}(u,v) =\left\langle u, \: v, \: {\color{black}\dfrac{2(v+3)}{u^2+1}} \right\rangle]

Therefore, the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{r}] is [MATH: {\color{black}\dfrac{2(v+3)}{u^2+1}}.]

Item 8 — Example: Finding a Parametrization of a Surface Defined in Cylindrical Polar Coordinates

Example Prompt:
[MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) =\big\langle r\cos{\theta}, \: r\sin{\theta}, \: \text{_____} \big\rangle]

The vector-valued function [MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta)] parametrizes the surface defined in cylindrical polar coordinates as
[MATH: {r^2}-4z^2=0]
for [MATH: z \geq 0.] What is the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we write the equation of the surface in the form [MATH: z=f(r,\theta)\mathbin{:}]

[MATH: r^{2} − 4z^{2}|= 0; 4z^{2}|= r^{2}; z^{2}|= (r^{2})/(4); z|= (r)/(2)]

We disregard the negative solution since we are given that [MATH: z\geq 0.]

If [MATH: (r, \theta, z)] are the cylindrical coordinates of a point and [MATH: (x,y,z)] are the corresponding Cartesian coordinates of that point, then we have

[MATH: x = r\cos\theta, \qquad
y = r\sin\theta, \qquad
z = z.]

Now, a point [MATH: (x,y,z)] on our surface has the corresponding position vector given by

[MATH: \mathbf{f} = \big\langle x, \: y, \: z \big\rangle = \big\langle r\cos\theta, \: r\sin\theta, \: z \big\rangle.]

Finally, substituting [MATH: z= \dfrac r2,] we obtain

[MATH: \mathbf{f}(r,\theta) =\left\langle r\cos{\theta}, \: r\sin{\theta}, \: {\color{black} \dfrac r2} \right\rangle.]

Therefore, the third component of [MATH: \mathbf{f}] is [MATH: {\color{black} \dfrac r2}.]
